name: Caṅkam (Sangam) literature
summary: The earliest corpus of Tamil poetry — the Eight Anthologies (Eṭṭuttokai) and Ten Idylls (Pattuppāṭṭu) — together with the grammar Tolkāppiyam, composed roughly between the turn of the era and the 5th–6th century CE, with later layers such as the Paripāṭal and Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai.
limits: The corpus is largely secular (akam love and puṟam heroic poetry); religious references are scattered and later poems are more devotional.

name: Tirumurai
summary: The twelve-book canon of Tamil Śaiva devotional literature: Tēvāram (1–7), Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (8), Tiruvicaippā and Tiruppallāṇṭu (9), Tirumūlar’s Tirumantiram (10), a miscellany including the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai (11) and Cēkkiḻār’s Periya Purāṇam (12).

dates.event: arrangement of books 1–11 (Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi) and addition of book 12
dates.label: c. late 10th – 12th c. CE
dates.basis: tradition of Nampi’s compilation; date of the Periya Purāṇam

name: Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās
summary: The scriptures of the Pāñcarātra tradition — traditionally 108, with over 200 known titles — including the Sāttvata, Pauṣkara and Jayākhya (“three gems”), the Ahirbudhnya, Pārameśvara, Īśvara and Lakṣmī Tantra.

dates.label: c. 7th–14th c. CE (disputed)
dates.basis: cross-citation and borrowing from Śaiva tantras

name: Śaiva Āgamas (Siddhānta tantras)
summary: The Sanskrit scriptures of the Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally twenty-eight Āgamas with subsidiary Upāgamas, beginning with the Kāmika; the earliest surviving tantra of the wider Mantramārga is the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā.

dates.event: composition of the surviving Siddhānta scriptures
dates.label: c. 5th–12th c. CE

limits: The South Indian “28 Āgamas” in current temple use are in part later recastings; the early Siddhānta canon is reconstructed largely from Nepalese manuscripts.

name: Śākta Tantras
summary: Tantras centred on the Goddess and her retinue (yoginīs, Kālī, Tripurasundarī, Kubjikā), including the Brahmayāmala (Picumata) of the early Vidyāpīṭha, the Kaula texts and later Śrīvidyā literature.

dates.label: c. 7th–15th c. CE
dates.basis: manuscripts and citation by Kashmirian authors

name: Maṅgalkāvya
summary: Bengali narrative poems (c. 13th–18th c.) celebrating the power of local or Purāṇic deities — Manasā, Caṇḍī, Dharma Ṭhākur, Annadā — and the establishment of their worship among reluctant devotees.

name: Sthala-purāṇas (temple and place legends)
summary: Texts recounting the sacred history of a particular shrine or town — its deity’s manifestation, divine marriages, miracles and royal patrons — in Sanskrit (often as māhātmyas within Purāṇas) and in Tamil and other languages.
details: Shulman (1980) analyses the Tamil talapurāṇams as a genre with recurring motifs (the goddess’s marriage, the self-manifested liṅga, the local flood myth). Their claims are evidence of temple tradition (class 6), not of the dates of the temples’ structures.
limits: A sthala-purāṇa’s account of a temple’s foundation is not a date for the surviving building.

name: Tolkāppiyam
summary: The oldest extant Tamil grammar and poetics, in three books (phonology, morphology, “subject-matter” — poruḷ). Its Akattiṇaiyiyal assigns presiding deities to the landscapes: Māyōṉ to the forest-pasture (mullai), Cēyōṉ to the hills (kuṟiñci), Vēntaṉ to farmland (marutam) and Varuṇaṉ to the shore (neytal).
details: Sūtra 5 of the Akattiṇaiyiyal reads: “māyōṉ mēya kāṭuṟai ulakamum / cēyōṉ mēya maivarai ulakamum / vēntaṉ mēya tīmpuṉal ulakamum / varuṇaṉ mēya perumaṇal ulakamum / mullai kuṟiñci marutam neytal eṉac / colliya muṟaiyāṟ collavum paṭumē.” The commentator Nacciṉārkkiṉiyar glosses Māyōṉ as “the one of sea-dark colour” (kaṭalvaṇṇaṉ) and Cēyōṉ as “red Murukaṉ.”
limits: The sūtra names Māyōṉ and Cēyōṉ; their glosses as Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa and Murukaṉ come from medieval commentators and modern scholarship.

name: Paripāṭal
summary: A late Caṅkam anthology (fifth of the Eight Anthologies) of musical poems: of the 24 that survive complete, 7 are addressed to Tirumāl (Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa), 8 to Murukaṉ (Cevvēḷ) and 9 to the river Vaikai at Madurai.
details: The poems to Murukaṉ celebrate the Tiruparaṅkuṉṟam hill near Madurai and know the Skanda birth story; the Tirumāl poems are among the earliest Tamil Vaiṣṇava devotional verse.

dates.label: c. 3rd–6th c. CE
dates.view: Vaiyapuri Pillai & Takahashi (3rd–4th c.); Ramanujan (c. 6th c.)

name: Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai
summary: Nakkīrar’s poem “guiding [the devotee] to Murukaṉ,” the first of the Ten Idylls and also included in Tirumurai 11. It describes six places where Murukaṉ is present and blends Tamil and northern (Skanda) imagery.
details: The poem (317 lines in the critical edition) uses the old guide-poem form, in which a bard directs another to a generous patron, now redirected to the god. Later tradition maps its six sites onto the six temples of the āṟupaṭai vīṭu.

dates.label: late Caṅkam (c. 3rd–6th c. CE); some scholars later

name: Tiruppāvai
summary: Āṇṭāḷ’s thirty Tamil verses in the voice of cowherd girls who rise before dawn in the month of Mārkaḻi to wake one another and Kṛṣṇa for a vow (nōṉpu). It is part of the Divya Prabandham and recited daily in Śrīvaiṣṇava worship.
details: The verses address Kṛṣṇa as born in “northern Mathurā” and living among the cowherds, and invoke Nappiṉṉai, his Tamil cowherd consort. Its title, with that of Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai, survives in the Thai royal Brahman ceremony Triyampawai–Trippawai (McGovern 2017).

name: Nācciyār Tirumoḻi
summary: Āṇṭāḷ’s 143 Tamil verses of longing for union with Viṣṇu–Kṛṣṇa, including the celebrated dream of her wedding to him (vāraṇam āyiram), part of the Divya Prabandham.

name: Tiruvāymoḻi
summary: Nammāḻvār’s 1,102-verse Tamil poem to Viṣṇu, in a hundred decads; Śrīvaiṣṇavas call it the Tamil (Drāviḍa) Veda and it was the subject of the first Śrīvaiṣṇava commentary, Piḷḷāṉ’s Āṟāyirappaṭi.

attributes.commentaries: Piḷḷāṉ’s Āṟāyirappaṭi (12th c.) and later maṇipravāḷa commentaries

name: Tiruvācakam
summary: Māṇikkavācakar’s Tamil hymns to Śiva, forming (with his Tirukkōvaiyār) Tirumurai book 8; intensely personal poems of grace, longing and Śiva as dancer at Tillai (Chidambaram).

name: Tiruvempāvai
summary: Māṇikkavācakar’s twenty-verse pāvai poem within the Tiruvācakam, in which young women wake each other at dawn in Mārkaḻi to bathe and praise Śiva — a Śaiva counterpart of Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai.

name: Tirumantiram
summary: Tirumūlar’s Tamil verse treatise on Śaiva doctrine, yoga and tantra (c. 3,000 verses), Tirumurai book 10, regarded as the earliest Tamil statement of Śaiva Siddhānta ideas; its date is much disputed.

name: Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam
summary: The Tamil sthala-purāṇa of Madurai narrating the sixty-four “sacred sports” (tiruviḷaiyāṭal) of Śiva as Cuntarēcuvarar, including his marriage to the warrior-princess Taṭātakai (Mīnākṣī). The best-known version is by Parañcōti Muṉivar.
details: Episodes include Mīnākṣī’s birth with three breasts and her conquest of the world until she meets Śiva at Kailāsa, Viṣṇu giving her in marriage, and stories involving Māṇikkavācakar (jackals turned into horses) and the Pāṇḍya kings. An earlier Tamil version is attributed to Perumpaṟṟappuliyūr Nampi, and the cycle has a Sanskrit counterpart in the Hālāsya Māhātmya.

dates.label: the reigns of the early (legendary) Pāṇḍya kings

limits: Temple-tradition narrative (class 6); it does not date the Mīnākṣī temple’s structures.

name: Kanta Purāṇam
summary: Kacciyappa Civācāriyar’s Tamil Skanda Purāṇa, recounting Murukaṉ’s birth and his war against the asura Cūrapatmaṉ (Śūrapadma), traditionally first recited at the Kumarakōṭṭam shrine in Kanchipuram.

attributes.author: Kacciyappa Civācāriyar
attributes.model text: Śaṅkara-saṃhitā of the Sanskrit Skanda Purāṇa (per tradition)

name: Āndhra Mahābhāratamu
summary: The Telugu Mahābhārata of the “poet trinity” (kavitrayam): Nannaya began it under the Eastern Cāḷukya king Rājarāja Narēndra (11th c.), Tikkana wrote fifteen books from the Virāṭa onward (13th c.), and Errana completed the Araṇya book (14th c.).

dates.event: Nannaya’s portion (Ādi, Sabhā, part of Araṇya)
dates.label: c. 1054–1061 CE

sources.locator: V. Narayana Rao, ch. on Telugu

name: Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇamu
summary: Telugu Rāmāyaṇa in dvipada couplets by Gona Budda Reddy (pen-name Raṅganātha), 13th–14th c. Its singable metre suited folk and puppet performance; it contains popular episodes absent from Vālmīki, such as the squirrel who helps build the bridge and Lakṣmaṇa drawing a protective line.

name: Āndhra Mahābhāgavatamu (Pōtana)
summary: Bammera Pōtana’s 15th-century Telugu rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, dedicated not to a king but to Rāma; much loved for its Gajendra-mokṣa and Kṛṣṇa narratives.

sources.locator: V. Narayana Rao, ch. on Telugu

name: Vikramārjuna Vijaya (Pampa Bhārata)
summary: The Kannada Mahābhārata in campū form by the Jain poet Pampa, completed c. 941 CE at the court of the Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya Arikēsari II; Pampa equates his patron with the hero Arjuna.
details: Pollock (2006) treats Pampa’s two works — the Jain Ādipurāṇa and this “worldly” (laukika) epic — as founding texts of cosmopolitan vernacular literature in Kannada. A Jain poet’s Mahābhārata, it is not a Jain purāṇa: it follows the Bhārata story while making Arjuna, rather than Yudhiṣṭhira, the crowned hero, an identification with the patron.

dates.label: c. 941 CE
dates.basis: internal dating of Pampa’s works (Ādipurāṇa 941; the epic shortly after, or c. 939–941)
dates.view: sources differ on the order of the two works

sources.locator: D. R. Nagaraj, ch. on Kannada

name: Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjarī (Gadugina Bhārata)
summary: Kumāravyāsa’s Kannada Mahābhārata (first ten books) in bhāminī ṣaṭpadi six-line stanzas, completed c. 1430 under the Vijayanagara king Dēvarāya II; it remains a living recitation text (gamaka) in Karnataka.
details: Local legend says it was composed in the Vīranārāyaṇa temple at Gadag, where a pillar bears the poet’s name.

sources.locator: D. R. Nagaraj, ch. on Kannada

name: Vacanas of Basavaṇṇa
summary: The free-verse Kannada sayings (vacana) attributed to Basava, addressed to Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, criticising temple ritual and caste and exalting the devotee’s body as Śiva’s temple.
limits: The vacanas were compiled long after Basava; individual attributions are uncertain.

name: Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu
summary: Eḻuttacchaṉ’s 16th-century Malayalam rendering of the Sanskrit Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa in the “parrot-song” form, in which a parrot recites the story; it is read aloud in Kerala households during the month of Karkkaṭakam.

name: Saptakāṇḍa Rāmāyaṇa (Assamese)
summary: Mādhava Kandali’s 14th-century Assamese rendering of Vālmīki, made for the Barāhī (Kachari) king Mahāmāṇikya — among the earliest renderings of a Sanskrit epic into a modern Indo-Aryan language. Its first and last books were lost and replaced in the 16th century by Mādhavadeva (Ādi) and Śaṅkaradeva (Uttara).
details: Kandali’s Rāma and Sītā are portrayed in human rather than divine terms, which later Vaiṣṇava readers considered unsuitable for devotional use — part of why Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva supplied new frame books.

name: Kīrtana Ghoṣā
summary: Śaṅkaradeva’s Assamese collection of devotional narrative songs, largely drawn from the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, the core scripture recited in the nāmghars and sattras of Ekaśaraṇa Vaiṣṇavism.

name: Śāraḷā Mahābhārata
summary: Śāraḷā Dāsa’s 15th-century Odia Mahābhārata, begun under the Gajapati Kapilendra Deva (r. 1435–1467). It follows the Bhārata outline but adds many episodes and Odia local colour, written in colloquial, unsanskritised Odia.

name: Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa
summary: Śāraḷā Dāsa’s Odia narrative of a war against a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa of the land of Vilaṅkā, after the defeat of the ten-headed one — a theme shared with the Sanskrit Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa’s Sahasra-Rāvaṇa.
openQuestions: Does Sītā (as goddess) or Rāma kill the thousand-headed Rāvaṇa in Śāraḷā’s text? Sources consulted say only “a battle between Rāma and the thousand-headed Rāvaṇa”.

name: Odia Bhāgabata
summary: Jagannātha Dāsa’s Odia rendering of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (late 15th – early 16th c.), in a simple nine-syllable metre; it became the most widely read devotional book of Odisha and the basis of village Bhāgabata-ghara reading houses.

dates.label: late 15th – early 16th c. CE
dates.basis: Jagannātha Dāsa’s association with Caitanya’s time at Puri

name: Manasāmaṅgal
summary: Bengali Maṅgalkāvya narratives of the snake goddess Manasā, centred on the merchant Cā̃d Sadāgar’s refusal to worship her and the devotion of his daughter-in-law Behulā, who wins back her dead husband Lakhindar.
details: Many poets composed Manasāmaṅgals; among the earliest named are Bijay Gupta and Bipradās Pipilāi (late 15th c.).

name: Caitanya Caritāmṛta
summary: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja’s Bengali–Sanskrit biography and theology of Caitanya (early 17th c.), which the Gauḍīya tradition treats as definitive; it presents Caitanya as Kṛṣṇa who took on the emotion and complexion of Rādhā.

name: Eknāthī Bhāgavata
summary: Eknāth’s Marathi ovī commentary on the eleventh book of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (the Uddhava-gītā), 16th c.

name: Tukārām Gāthā
summary: The collection of Marathi abhaṅgas attributed to Tukārām (traditionally c. 4,500), sung by Vārkarī pilgrims on the road to Pandharpur.
limits: Manuscripts are unsystematic collections; individual abhaṅgas cannot all be securely attributed.

name: Sūrsāgar
summary: The “Ocean of Sūr”: the corpus of Braj Bhāṣā songs attributed to Sūrdās, chiefly on Kṛṣṇa’s childhood and the love of Rādhā and the gopīs, arranged in later recensions in twelve books after the Bhāgavata. Most of the received corpus is later than Sūr; Hawley and Bryant reconstruct an early core from manuscripts.
details: The earliest dated manuscript containing poems in Sūr’s name is reported by Hawley as the Fatehpur manuscript of VS 1639 (1582 CE); it contains a few hundred poems, far fewer than the thousands of the later vulgate.

dates.label: 1582 CE (VS 1639)
dates.basis: manuscript colophon as reported by Hawley (not checked in this session)

limits: Attribution of individual songs to Sūrdās is mostly uncertain.

name: Hanumān Cālīsā
summary: Forty-verse Awadhi hymn to Hanumān, traditionally attributed to Tulsīdās and now the most widely recited Hindu devotional hymn in North India.
limits: The attribution to Tulsīdās is traditional; Lutgendorf (2007) notes it is not secure.

name: Vākhs of Lal Ded
summary: Kashmiri four-line mystical sayings (vākh) attributed to the 14th-century yoginī Lal Ded (Lallā), venerated by Hindus as Lalleśvarī and by Muslims as Lal ʿĀrifa; they survived orally and were first written down systematically in the 20th century.
limits: Recorded from oral tradition some six centuries after her lifetime; attributions are uncertain.

name: Gāhā Sattasaī
summary: An anthology of 700 Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit love verses attributed to the Sātavāhana king Hāla; dated between the 1st and 7th centuries (before Bāṇa, 7th c.). One verse mentions Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā, the earliest known literary mention of her.

dates.label: c. 3rd–4th c. CE
dates.basis: language; cited by Bāṇa before 640 CE

dates.label: by King Hāla (1st c. CE in tradition)

limits: The verses circulated in recensions; a given verse may be later than the anthology’s core.

name: Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa
summary: A Sanskrit Śākta-inflected Rāma narrative in 27 sargas framed as a secret telling by Vālmīki to Bharadvāja. Sītā is born to Mandodarī, and in the climax she takes the form of Mahākālī and destroys the thousand-headed Sahasra-Rāvaṇa after Rāma falls unconscious.
openQuestions: A secure date is lacking; scholarly study of the text has been minor.

name: Bhaṭṭikāvya (Rāvaṇavadha)
summary: Bhaṭṭi’s 6th–7th-century Sanskrit mahākāvya telling the Rāma story while illustrating the rules of Pāṇini’s grammar; it was the model for the first half of the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa.

name: Uttarapurāṇa of Guṇabhadra
summary: The 9th-century Digambara Jain Sanskrit universal history completing Jinasena’s Ādipurāṇa; its Rāma section follows a different Jain line from Vimalasūri, making Sītā the daughter of Rāvaṇa and Mandodarī, abandoned at birth because of a prophecy.

name: Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra
summary: A Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra (c. 4th–5th c.) whose frame story has the Buddha visiting Laṅkā at the invitation of its king Rāvaṇa, who questions him on the dharma.
limits: Its Rāvaṇa is a devout questioner; the sūtra does not narrate the Rāmāyaṇa story.

name: Hikayat Seri Rama (Malay)
summary: The Malay prose Rāma narrative, put into its present form between the 13th and 17th centuries, with Islamic framing in some versions (Dasaratha as a descendant of the prophet Adam). Its oldest manuscript, in the Bodleian Library, was acquired by Archbishop Laud by 1633.
details: Characters: Seri Rama, Siti Dewi (Sītā), Laksamana, Maharaja Wana (Rāvaṇa), Hanuman Kera Putih. A related shadow-play repertoire (Hikayat Maharaja Wana) was among the most important wayang kulit tellings of the Malay peninsula.

name: Yama Zatdaw (Burmese)
summary: The Burmese Rāma tradition (Yamayana), known in Bagan-period terracottas as the Dasaratha Jātaka and in literature from a 1527 pyo poem; it was reshaped in the Konbaung period by Thai court drama brought back after the conquest of Ayutthaya.
details: Names: Yama (Rāma), Me Thida (Sītā), Lakkhana, Dasagiri (Rāvaṇa). Often called Myanmar’s unofficial national epic.

name: Phra Lak Phra Lam (Lao)
summary: The Lao Rāma epic, framed as a jātaka: Phra Lam is a previous birth of the Buddha, and Rāvaṇa (Hapmanasouane) is his cousin, compared with Devadatta or Māra. Versions were recorded on palm leaf from the 15th to the early 19th century.
details: Nang Sida is the daughter of Thôtsakane (Rāvaṇa) and Nang Chanta in the Lao character lists — another telling where Sītā is Rāvaṇa’s daughter.

name: Jayākhya Saṃhitā
summary: One of the “three gems” of the Pāñcarātra canon, a ritual and theological saṃhitā edited in 1931; its date is disputed, from an early proposal of c. 5th c. to later scholarship placing it around the 8th–9th c.

name: Sāttvata Saṃhitā
summary: Among the oldest and most authoritative Pāñcarātra saṃhitās (one of the “three gems”), with a commentary by Alaśiṅga Bhaṭṭa; date disputed.

name: Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā
summary: Pāñcarātra saṃhitā known for its doctrine of the Sudarśana (Viṣṇu’s discus) and its cosmology; the subject of Schrader’s pioneering 1916 study, which placed it early, a dating later scholars question.

name: Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā
summary: The earliest surviving tantra of the Śaiva Mantramārga, in five books; its editors date the oldest layer (Mūlasūtra) to c. 450–550 CE. It preserves an early stage of Śaiva Siddhānta ritual and the transition from the Atimārga.

dates.label: c. 450–550 CE
dates.basis: internal evidence; relationship to Pāśupata and Purāṇic material

name: Brahmayāmala (Picumata)
summary: An early Vidyāpīṭha tantra of the Bhairava stream, centred on Kapālīśabhairava and the goddess Caṇḍā Kāpālinī with their yoginīs; studied by Hatley as a key source for early Śākta-Śaiva yoginī cults.

dates.label: c. 7th–9th c. CE
dates.basis: Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript evidence and internal evidence

name: Civañāṉapōtam (Śivajñānabodham)
summary: Meykaṇṭār’s 13th-century twelve-sūtra Tamil treatise that founded the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta school; tradition calls it a rendering of twelve Sanskrit verses from the Raurava Āgama, a claim scholars treat cautiously.

name: Tantrāloka
summary: Abhinavagupta’s encyclopaedic Sanskrit exposition of Trika Śaiva ritual and doctrine (c. 1000 CE), in thirty-seven chapters, based above all on the Mālinīvijayottara Tantra.

name: Nāthamuni
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya (9th–10th c.) of Vīranārāyaṇapuram (Kāṭṭumaṉṉārkōyil), credited with collecting and arranging the Nālāyira Divya Prabandham and setting it to music; grandfather of Yāmuna.

name: Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-compiler of Tirunāraiyūr (10th–11th c.) who arranged the Tēvāram and other hymns into the first eleven books of the Tirumurai; tradition links his work to Rājarāja I.

name: Māṇikkavācakar
summary: Tamil Śaiva poet-saint, author of the Tiruvācakam and Tirukkōvaiyār (Tirumurai 8); hagiography makes him a minister of a Pāṇḍya king who renounced office after meeting Śiva at Tirupperuntuṟai. Most scholars place him in the 9th century, though earlier dates are proposed.

name: Cēkkiḻār
summary: Tamil poet and minister at the court of the Cōḻa king Kulōttuṅka II (12th c.), author of the Periya Purāṇam.

name: Nakkīrar
summary: Tamil poet to whom the Tirumurukāṟṟuppaṭai is attributed; tradition (including the Tiruviḷaiyāṭal Purāṇam) makes him the president of the Madurai academy (caṅkam) who dared to challenge Śiva’s poem.

dates.label: late Caṅkam (c. 3rd–6th c. CE)
dates.basis: date of the poem; several poets of the name may be conflated

name: Iḷaṅkō Aṭikaḷ
summary: The “venerable prince-ascetic,” brother of the Cēra king Ceṅkuṭṭuvaṉ according to the prologue of the Cilappatikāram, to whom the epic is attributed; the attribution rests on a later prologue and is doubted.
limits: Historicity and authorship uncertain.

name: Periyāḻvār
summary: Āḻvār of Śrīvilliputtūr (8th–9th c.), author of the Periyāḻvār Tirumoḻi with its celebrated poems of Kṛṣṇa’s infancy and of the Tiruppallāṇṭu; foster-father of Āṇṭāḷ.

name: Nannaya
summary: Telugu poet (11th c.), “first poet” (ādikavi) of Telugu, who began the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu at the request of the Eastern Cāḷukya king Rājarāja Narēndra.

name: Tikkana
summary: Telugu poet and minister (13th c.) who rendered fifteen books (Virāṭa to Svargārohaṇa) of the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu.

name: Errana
summary: Telugu poet (14th c.) at the court of Prolaya Vēma Reḍḍi who completed the Araṇya book of the Āndhra Mahābhāratamu.

name: Gona Budda Reddy (Raṅganātha)
summary: Telugu poet (13th–14th c.), author under the pen-name Raṅganātha of the dvipada Raṅganātha Rāmāyaṇamu.

name: Bammera Pōtana
summary: Telugu poet (15th c.) of Bammera near Warangal, author of the Āndhra Mahābhāgavatamu, who according to tradition refused to dedicate his work to the king of Rācakoṇḍa and offered it to Rāma.

name: Pampa (Ādikavi Pampa)
summary: Jain Kannada poet (902–c. 955) at the Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya court of Arikēsari II, author of the Ādipurāṇa (941) and the Vikramārjuna Vijaya.

name: Kumāravyāsa
summary: Kannada poet (Nāraṇappa, early 15th c.) of Gadag, author of the Karṇāṭa Bhārata Kathāmañjarī, active under Dēvarāya II of Vijayanagara.

name: Tuñcattu Rāmānujaṉ Eḻuttacchaṉ
summary: Malayalam poet (16th c.), called the father of modern Malayalam literature, author of the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇam Kiḷippāṭṭu and a Mahābhāratam Kiḷippāṭṭu.

dates.label: c. 1495–1575 CE (Ulloor); 16th–17th c. in other views

name: Mādhava Kandali
summary: Assamese poet (14th c.) who rendered Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa into Assamese for the Barāhī king Mahāmāṇikya.

name: Śrīmanta Śaṅkaradeva
summary: Assamese saint, poet, dramatist and founder of Ekaśaraṇa Vaiṣṇavism (1449–1568), author of the Kīrtana Ghoṣā, the Aṅkīyā Nāṭ one-act plays and the Bargīt songs, and of the Uttara kāṇḍa of the Assamese Rāmāyaṇa.

name: Mādhavadeva
summary: Assamese poet and chief disciple of Śaṅkaradeva (16th c.), author of the Nām Ghoṣā and of the Ādi kāṇḍa of the Assamese Rāmāyaṇa.

name: Śāraḷā Dāsa
summary: Odia poet (15th c.) of the reign of the Gajapati Kapilendra Deva, author of the Odia Mahābhārata, the Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa and the Caṇḍī Purāṇa; his name, “by the grace of Sāraḷā,” refers to his goddess.

name: Jagannātha Dāsa
summary: Odia poet (late 15th – 16th c.) of Puri, one of the Pañcasakhā, author of the Odia Bhāgabata and founder of the Atibaḍī tradition.

name: Eknāth
summary: Marathi poet-saint of Paiṭhaṇ (c. 1533–1599), author of the Eknāthī Bhāgavata and the Bhāvārtha Rāmāyaṇa, who produced a corrected text of the Jñāneśvarī in 1584.

name: Tukārām
summary: Marathi poet-saint of Dehū (1608 or 1598 – 1649/1650), a grocer by caste whose abhaṅgas to Viṭṭhala are central to the Vārkarī pilgrimage.

dates.label: 1598/1608 – 1649/1650 CE
dates.basis: competing reconstructions; death in 1650 widely accepted

name: Nāmdev
summary: Marathi poet-saint (traditionally 1270–1350), a tailor of Pandharpur, devotee of Viṭṭhala and contemporary of Jñāneśvar; songs attributed to him are also in the Sikh Ādi Granth.

name: Sūrdās
summary: Braj Bhāṣā poet-singer of the 16th century to whom the Sūrsāgar is attributed; hagiography makes him blind and a disciple of Vallabha, claims modern scholarship treats as later constructions.

name: Lal Ded (Lalleśvarī)
summary: Kashmiri yoginī-poet of the 14th century, revered by Hindus as Lalleśvarī and by Muslims as Lal ʿĀrifa, to whom the vākhs are attributed.

name: Narsinh Mehtā
summary: Gujarati poet-saint of Junagadh (c. 1414 – 1480s), honoured as the Ādi Kavi of Gujarati, devotee of Kṛṣṇa and author of the bhajan “Vaiṣṇava jana to.”

name: Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja
summary: Gauḍīya poet-theologian of Vṛndāvana (16th–17th c.), author of the Caitanya Caritāmṛta.

name: Meykaṇṭār
summary: Tamil Śaiva theologian (13th c.) of Tiruveṇṇainallūr, author of the Civañāṉapōtam and founder of the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta lineage.

name: Abhinavagupta
summary: Kashmirian Śaiva philosopher and aesthetician (fl. c. 975–1025), author of the Tantrāloka, of commentaries on Utpaladeva’s Pratyabhijñā and of the Abhinavabhāratī on the Nāṭyaśāstra.

name: Rama I (Phutthayotfa Chulalok)
summary: First king of the Chakri dynasty of Siam (r. 1782–1809), founder of Bangkok, under whom the canonical Ramakien was compiled (1797–1807), partly by the king himself.

name: Kulōttuṅka Cōḻa II
summary: Cōḻa king (r. 1133–1150) at whose court Cēkkiḻār composed the Periya Purāṇam; Śaiva tradition associates him with the expansion of the Chidambaram temple.

name: Lakṣmaṇasena
summary: King of the Sena dynasty of Bengal (r. c. 1178–1206), at whose court tradition places Jayadeva together with the poets Umāpatidhara, Śaraṇa, Govardhana and Dhoyī.

name: Arikēsari II
summary: Vēmulavāḍa Cāḷukya ruler (10th c.), a feudatory of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa Kṛṣṇa III, patron of Pampa, who equated him with Arjuna in the Vikramārjuna Vijaya.

name: Viṭṭhala (Viṭhobā) of Pandharpur
summary: The deity of Pandharpur in Maharashtra, standing with hands on hips upon a brick, worshipped by Vārkarīs as a form of Kṛṣṇa/Viṣṇu; scholars debate his origins (pastoral hero-stone, Jain, Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava elements).
details: The Puṇḍalīka legend explains the brick: Kṛṣṇa came to the devotee Puṇḍalīka, who, busy serving his parents, threw him a brick to stand on, and the god remains standing there. Dhere (2011) reads Viṭṭhala as an amalgam of pastoral hero-gods of the Dhangar herders absorbed into Kṛṣṇa devotion; Deleury suggested a hero-stone origin. A monument dated 1189 and a Hoysala inscription of 1237 are the earliest dated references noted in the literature.

dates.label: 1189 (monument) and 1237 CE (inscription)
dates.basis: inscriptions as reported in secondary literature

limits: Inscriptions attest worship at Pandharpur by the late 12th–13th c.; they do not settle the deity’s origins.

name: Māyōṉ (Tamil)
summary: The “dark one,” presiding deity of the mullai (forest-pasture) landscape in the Tolkāppiyam, and in Caṅkam poetry a dark cowherd god (also called Māl, Tirumāl) later identified with Viṣṇu and Kṛṣṇa. Kept distinct from deity:vishnu and joined by IDENTIFIED_WITH.
details: Hardy (1983) argues that the Tamil cowherd god of the mullai landscape, with his beloved Piññai and his dances with cowherd girls, contributed to the emotional (viraha) bhakti later expressed by the Āḻvārs and, through the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, to pan-Indian Kṛṣṇa devotion.
limits: The name Māyōṉ in the sūtra does not by itself establish a theology identical with Sanskrit Viṣṇu.

name: Nappiṉṉai (Piññai)
summary: The Tamil cowherd girl beloved of Kṛṣṇa (Māyavaṉ) in the Cilappatikāram’s round-dance of the cowherdesses and in the Āḻvārs’ hymns, where she is his consort; some scholars see her as a southern parallel or precursor of Rādhā, others identify her with Nīḷā Devī.
limits: Whether Piññai and Rādhā share an origin is a scholarly hypothesis; the texts keep them apart.

name: Vaḷḷi
summary: Murukaṉ’s Tamil consort, a hunter (kuṟava) girl of the hills whom the god woos in disguise; she stands beside Teyvāṉai (Devasenā), daughter of Indra, in Tamil tradition.

name: Suvannamaccha
summary: Mermaid princess, daughter of Thotsakan (Rāvaṇa), in Thai and other Southeast Asian Rāma tellings; sent to sabotage the causeway to Laṅkā, she falls in love with Hanumān and bears him a son, Macchanu.
limits: Absent from Vālmīki; a Southeast Asian figure.

name: Macchanu
summary: Son of Hanumān and the mermaid Suvannamaccha in the Ramakien, half monkey and half fish, who later meets and fights his father before they recognise each other.

name: Thotsakan
summary: The ten-faced king of Laṅkā in the Thai Ramakien — the counterpart of Rāvaṇa (the name renders Daśakaṇṭha) — who in this telling is the father of Sida, keeps his heart outside his body, and dies when Hanumān crushes it.
limits: Kept separate from char:ravana because the Ramakien gives him a different family and fate; identified with Rāvaṇa by an assertion.

name: Māyā-Sītā (the illusory Sītā)
summary: The illusory double or reflection of Sītā who, in the Kūrma Purāṇa, Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa, Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa and Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas, is the one Rāvaṇa abducts while the real Sītā is kept safe in Agni.
details: In the Mānas Rāma says: “tumha pāvaka mahuṃ karahu nivāsā, jau lagi karauṃ nisācara nāsā” (“dwell in the fire until I destroy the night-rovers”) and Sītā leaves “nija pratibimba,” her own reflection, “of the same character, form and modesty”; not even Lakṣmaṇa knows. At the fire-ordeal the reflection and the worldly stain burn in the fire and Agni returns the true Śrī to Rāma. Doniger (1999) traces the motif’s development and its theological work: protecting Sītā’s purity and recasting the ordeal.
limits: A theological and narrative motif of particular texts; not present in Vālmīki’s Rāmāyaṇa.

name: Bhāmaṇḍala
summary: In Jain Rāma tellings (Vimalasūri’s Paumacariya and successors), Sītā’s twin brother, carried off at birth and raised as a vidyādhara prince, who falls in love with Sītā from her portrait and seeks her hand before learning that she is his twin sister.

name: Sahasra-Rāvaṇa (the thousand-headed Rāvaṇa)
summary: A thousand-headed elder brother or double of Rāvaṇa who, in the Adbhuta Rāmāyaṇa, is destroyed by Sītā in the form of Mahākālī after Rāma is struck down; a thousand-headed Rāvaṇa is also fought in Śāraḷā Dāsa’s Odia Vilaṅkā Rāmāyaṇa.

name: Kaṇṇaki
summary: Heroine of the Cilappatikāram, who proves her executed husband Kōvalaṉ innocent before the Pāṇḍya king, burns Madurai with her curse and is deified as the chaste goddess Pattiṉi, worshipped in Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Sri Lanka.

name: Pandharpur
summary: Town on the Bhīmā (Candrabhāgā) river in Maharashtra, seat of the Viṭṭhala temple and goal of the Vārkarī pilgrimages (vārī) of Āṣāḍha and Kārttika.

name: Śrīvilliputtūr
summary: Temple town in Virudhunagar district, Tamil Nadu, home of Periyāḻvār and Āṇṭāḷ according to tradition, with twin shrines of Āṇṭāḷ and Vaṭapatrasāyī (Raṅganātha).

location.label: Srivilliputhur, Virudhunagar district, Tamil Nadu, India

name: Nevāsā
summary: Town on the Pravarā near its confluence with the Godāvarī (Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra), identified by tradition as the place where the Jñāneśvarī was composed, home of the Mohinīrāja (Mahālayā) temple named in the colophon.
limits: The colophon names the Godāvarī bank and Śrī Mahālayā; the identification with Nevāsā is traditional.

name: Vārkarī
summary: The Marathi devotional tradition of Viṭṭhala of Pandharpur, carried by pilgrims (vārkarī) who walk to Pandharpur twice a year singing the abhaṅgas of Jñāneśvar, Nāmdev, Eknāth, Tukārām and other saints.

name: Ekaśaraṇa Dharma
summary: The Assamese Vaiṣṇava movement founded by Śaṅkaradeva (15th–16th c.): exclusive refuge in Kṛṣṇa through congregational singing and hearing of his name and deeds, organised in sattras and village nāmghars; Rādhā is not worshipped alongside Kṛṣṇa.

name: Puṣṭimārga
summary: The Kṛṣṇa tradition founded by Vallabha (16th c.), centred on Śrīnāthjī and the “eight seals” (aṣṭachāp) of poets, among whom it counts Sūrdās.

name: Rāmānandī
summary: The North Indian Vaiṣṇava ascetic order tracing itself to Rāmānanda, centred on Rāma and Sītā; it claims Tulsīdās and is traditionally associated with the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa.

name: Rāmlīlā
summary: North Indian staged performance of the Rāma story based on Tulsīdās’s Rāmcaritmānas, held around Dussehra over ten to twelve days or (at Ramnagar, Varanasi) a month; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2005).
details: UNESCO names the Rāmlīlās of Ayodhyā, Ramnagar, Banaras, Vṛndāvan, Almora, Sattna and Madhubani as the most representative. Lutgendorf (1991) describes the Ramnagar Rāmlīlā patronised by the Mahārājā of Banaras as an environmental performance in which the audience moves with the action across the town.

name: Kūṭiyāṭṭam
summary: Sanskrit theatre of Kerala performed by Cākyār and Nampyār families in temple theatres (kūttampalam), with long elaborations of single acts of Sanskrit plays (including Rāma plays); inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2001).

name: Yakṣagāna
summary: Dance-drama of coastal Karnataka, led by a singer-narrator (bhāgavata), performing episodes (prasaṅga) from the Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata; an inscription of 1556 at Kurugodu records land given to performers.

dates.label: 1556 CE
dates.basis: inscription as reported in secondary literature

name: Kathakaḷi
summary: Kerala dance-drama that crystallised in the 16th–17th centuries from Rāmanāṭṭam (attributed to the Kottarakkara Tampurāṉ) and Kṛṣṇanāṭṭam (of the Zamorin Mānavēdaṉ), performing Rāmāyaṇa, Mahābhārata and Bhāgavata stories.

name: Wayang
summary: Indonesian puppet and shadow theatre (wayang kulit and related forms) led by a dalang with gamelan, performing stories from the Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa among others; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2003).

name: Khon
summary: Thai masked dance-drama performing episodes of the Ramakien, historically a court art; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2018 as “Khon, masked dance drama in Thailand.”

name: Royal Ballet of Cambodia
summary: Khmer classical court dance, whose repertoire includes Reamker episodes; inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List in 2008 (proclaimed 2003).
limits: The UNESCO record itself does not name the Reamker; the repertoire link rests on secondary literature.

name: Triyampawai–Trippawai ceremony
summary: Thai royal Brahman new-year ceremony (December–January) whose name comes from two Tamil devotional poems — Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai and Āṇṭāḷ’s Tiruppāvai — and during which hymns from these collections are chanted; it was historically linked to the Giant Swing in Bangkok.
details: McGovern (2017) writes that “Trīyampawāi is a corruption of Māṇikkavācakar’s Tiruvempāvai, and Trīppawāi is likewise a corruption of Āṇḍāḷ’s Tiruppāvai,” and reports Tamil texts in Thai and Grantha scripts in the National Library, Bangkok, together with recordings of the hymns sung in the ceremony. The present court Brahmans speak no Indian language.
limits: Shows the circulation of Tamil hymn names and texts into Thai court ritual; it does not show when or by whom they were brought.

name: Cāḷukyas of Vēmulavāḍa
summary: A 9th–10th-century dynasty in northern Telangana, feudatories of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas, patrons of the Kannada poet Pampa under Arikēsari II.

name: Rattanakosin Kingdom (Chakri dynasty)
summary: The Siamese kingdom ruled from Bangkok by the Chakri dynasty from 1782, under whose first kings the Ramakien was compiled and the Wat Phra Kaew murals painted.

name: Sena dynasty of Bengal
summary: Dynasty ruling Bengal in the 11th–13th centuries, whose king Lakṣmaṇasena is traditionally Jayadeva’s patron.

name: The Prambanan Rāmāyaṇa reliefs illustrate the Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa
summary: The claim that the 9th-century Rāmāyaṇa reliefs on the Śiva and Brahmā temples at Prambanan follow the Old Javanese Kakawin. Since Stutterheim (1925) scholars have noted episodes that diverge from the Kakawin and suggest another, possibly oral, telling.
limits: Both the reliefs and the poem belong to the Medang period; contemporaneity does not establish that one illustrates the other.

name: Sūrdās was a disciple of Vallabha
summary: The Puṣṭimārga hagiographic claim (Caurāsī Vaiṣṇavan kī Vārtā) that Sūrdās was initiated by Vallabha and became one of the aṣṭachāp poets; Hawley argues the connection is a later sectarian construction.

name: Basava founded the Vīraśaiva / Liṅgāyata tradition
summary: The traditional claim that Basava founded the Liṅgāyata community; modern scholars using Kalacuri-period inscriptions and the vacana corpus often see him as a reformer and organiser of an existing Śaiva milieu.

name: The Dasaratha Jātaka preserves an older form of the Rāma story than Vālmīki
summary: Argued in the 19th century (notably by Albrecht Weber) because of the jātaka’s simpler plot and sibling-marriage motif; most later scholars regard it as a Buddhist reworking of a story already known in Rāmāyaṇa form, though its verses may be old.
